text: Alright, today we're setting up a complete PCB etching process in our electronics lab. First, I need to put together the etching station that Sarah prepared earlier this morning. The copper-clad fiberglass board that we'll be working with today was cut to exactly 4.2 inches by 3.1 inches using our precision shear. Now, let me heat up the ferric chloride solution to the optimal temperature of 125 degrees Fahrenheit - this solution, which has been mixed to a concentration of 42%, needs to reach this temperature before we can start. While the chemical bath heats up, I'm going to set up the photoresist application station on the main workbench. The UV-sensitive photoresist film that was delivered yesterday will be applied using our laminating roller, and then the circuit pattern will be transferred onto the board. After that, the exposed photoresist is removed by the developer solution in approximately 90 seconds. Next, I'll hook up the bubble agitation system - this creates the movement that speeds up the etching process. The etching itself takes about 12 minutes, during which the unwanted copper gets eaten away by the heated ferric chloride. Finally, the remaining photoresist is stripped off using acetone, and we end up with our finished PCB that weighs roughly 28 grams. The experienced technician with 15 years of PCB fabrication experience always checks the trace width, which should measure 0.8 millimeters for this particular design.
